<description>
{
 "summary": "Rewrites the `torcontrol` fuzz target to drive a real `TorControlConnection` over a mocked `DynSock` socket connected to a simulated Tor daemon instead of directly invoking controller callbacks. The mock Tor daemon generates valid wire replies for PROTOCOLINFO, SAFECOOKIE authentication, GETINFO, and ADD_ONION, while asserting that sent commands use offered auth methods, use fresh nonces, and maintain valid port mappings. It also fixes a bug in `DynSock::Wait()` where wrapping `this` in an owning `std::shared_ptr` caused the socket to delete itself.",
 "problem": "The existing fuzz harness bypassed wire-level parsing (`ProcessBuffer()`, `ReceiveAndProcess()`) by invoking internal callbacks directly with dummy strings capped at 16 characters. It could not forge cryptographic responses such as SAFECOOKIE HMACs or v3 onion checksums, leaving most handshake and success paths unreachable. In addition, `DynSock::Wait()` was unusable because it destroyed its own socket instance on return.",
 "evidence": [

  "Commit 4fb5840f8e: 'Wait() wrapped `this` in an owning shared_ptr to call WaitMany(), so the socket was deleted once that temporary went out of scope.'"
 ],

<category name="tests" title="Test infrastructure">
## Covers

The machinery of testing rather than tests of a particular area: the
functional test framework and runner, unit test utilities, the fuzzing
harnesses and corpora, benchmarks, linters, sanitizer configuration,
and fixes for flaky tests whose cause is in the framework. A test that
pins the behavior of one area (a wallet migration test, a p2p relay
test) belongs to that area, not here. The Tests and Fuzzing labels are
a prior, but a labeled PR whose tests are about one area goes to that
area instead.

## What matters here

Signal first: fixes for flaky or misleading tests, since a red CI that
nobody trusts hides real failures. Then coverage of high-risk code paths
that the fuzzers or functional tests do not reach, especially
consensus, mempool policy, and p2p message handling. Then framework
capabilities that unblock tests other areas need. Then test speed, which
every contributor pays for on every run. Then cleanliness of the test
code.

Adding tests for their own sake ranks low; adding a test that catches a
realistic regression ranks high.
